title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela

pages.title: Let the model look things up

blocks.html: The problem. A large language model stores facts in its weights — but that knowledge is parametric: baked in, implicit, impossible to inspect, hard to update, and impossible to cite. Ask such a model a factual question and it will answer confidently whether or not it actually knows. That structural inability to say 'let me check' is the root cause of hallucination.

An analogy. A closed-book exam taken from memory versus an open-book exam where you can flip to the relevant page. A pure language model is always taking the closed-book exam. RAG hands it the book and lets it look up the passage before answering — and the passage is right there to cite.

The architecture. RAG couples a pre-trained generator (BART, a sequence-to-sequence Transformer) with a retriever (Dense Passage Retrieval) that searches an external corpus (all of Wikipedia, ~21 million 100-word passages). Given a query, the retriever pulls the top-$k$ relevant passages; the generator then writes its answer conditioned on the query and those passages.

The key technical move. The retrieved document is treated as a latent variable that is marginalized out — summed over — and the retriever and generator are fine-tuned jointly. This means the retriever learns to fetch documents that the generator actually finds useful for producing the right answer, not merely documents that look superficially similar to the query.

Why it is in the collection. 'Add RAG' became the default way to ground LLMs in private or up-to-date data. The specific 2020 architecture has been superseded, but the framing — retrieval as a first-class, trainable component with documents as latent variables — is the conceptual foundation of the entire retrieval-augmentation field.

pages.title: The two components: DPR retriever + BART generator

blocks.html: The retriever — Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR). Two separate BERT encoders. A passage encoder $d(z)$ turns each document $z$ into a fixed dense vector; a query encoder $q(x)$ turns the input query $x$ into a vector of the same size. Relevance is just their dot product $d(z)^\top q(x)$ — high when the vectors point the same way.

Reading it term by term: $p_\eta(z|x)$ is the probability the retriever assigns to document $z$ given query $x$; $\eta$ are the retriever's parameters; $d(z)$ and $q(x)$ are the passage and query embedding vectors (768-dimensional); their dot product scores the match; $\exp$ and the proportionality turn the top-scoring documents into a probability distribution (a softmax over candidates). To make this fast over 21M passages, all $d(z)$ are pre-computed offline and stored in a FAISS index, which finds the top-$k$ nearest neighbors in milliseconds.

The generator — BART. A pre-trained encoder-decoder Transformer (400M params). Its input is the query $x$ concatenated with one retrieved passage $z$; its output is the answer $y$, generated token by token. Formally it models $p_\theta(y \mid x, z)$, the probability of answer $y$ given the query and that document.

A concrete example. Query: 'Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?' DPR retrieves the Wikipedia passage on Jane Austen; BART reads 'query: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice? document: Pride and Prejudice is an 1813 novel by Jane Austen...' and generates 'Jane Austen.' The answer is grounded in a retrieved, inspectable source.

pages.title: Marginalizing over documents: RAG-Sequence vs RAG-Token

blocks.html: The core question. The retriever returns $k$ documents, not one. How should all $k$ contribute to the answer? RAG never commits to a single document — it treats the document as a hidden (latent) variable and averages over the top-$k$, weighting each by how relevant the retriever thinks it is. There are two ways to do this averaging.
RAG-Sequence: pick one document and use it for the entire answer, then marginalize across documents at the level of the whole sequence:

blocks.tex: p_{\text{RAG-Seq}}(y \mid x) = \sum_{z \in \text{top-}k} p_\eta(z \mid x)\; p_\theta(y \mid x, z)

blocks.html: Reading it term by term: the sum runs over the top-$k$ retrieved documents; $p_\eta(z|x)$ is the retriever's weight for document $z$; $p_\theta(y|x,z)$ is the probability the generator assigns to the full answer $y$ using only document $z$. Each candidate document produces a complete answer probability, and they are blended by retrieval weight. One document is responsible for the whole output.
RAG-Token: let each token of the answer draw on a possibly different document, marginalizing per token:

blocks.tex: p_{\text{RAG-Tok}}(y \mid x) = \prod_{i}^{N} \sum_{z \in \text{top-}k} p_\eta(z \mid x)\; p_\theta(y_i \mid x, z, y_{1:i-1})

blocks.html: Reading it term by term: the outer product $\prod_i$ runs over the $N$ answer tokens; for each token position $i$, the inner sum marginalizes over documents; $p_\theta(y_i | x, z, y_{1:i-1})$ is the probability of the next token $y_i$ given the query, document $z$, and the tokens generated so far $y_{1:i-1}$. Because the document is re-marginalized at every token, token 1 can come mostly from document A and token 5 mostly from document B.

When to use which. RAG-Sequence is better for answers that come from a single source — open-domain QA, Jeopardy answers — where one document holds the whole fact. RAG-Token shines when an answer stitches together facts from several documents (e.g. 'list the capitals of three countries'), since different parts of the output can be sourced independently.

pages.title: Training: how the retriever learns without re-indexing

blocks.html: The objective. Train the whole system end-to-end to maximize the likelihood of the correct answer — i.e. minimize the negative log-likelihood of $y$ given $x$, using the marginalized $p(y|x)$ above. Crucially, no labels are needed for which document is correct: the document is latent, and the model figures out which documents help purely from whether they lead to the right answer.

Reading it: the sum is over training (query, answer) pairs; $p(y|x)$ is the marginal answer probability (RAG-Sequence or RAG-Token); the negative log of it is the standard cross-entropy loss. Gradient flows into the generator $\theta$ directly, and into the retriever $\eta$ through the weights $p_\eta(z|x)$ — documents that contributed to correct answers get their retrieval probability pushed up.

The clever shortcut. Updating the retriever would normally mean re-embedding all 21M Wikipedia passages after every gradient step (to keep the FAISS index consistent) — astronomically expensive. RAG sidesteps this: it freezes the passage encoder $d(z)$ (so the index never changes) and only trains the query encoder $q(x)$ and the generator. The retriever improves by learning to map queries into the fixed document-embedding space such that useful documents land nearby — not by moving the documents.

Why this works. Empirically, fine-tuning only the query side recovers most of the benefit of full joint training at a tiny fraction of the cost. It is the practical compromise that makes end-to-end retrieval training feasible at all.

pages.title: QA, fact verification, and the killer feature: hot-swappable knowledge

blocks.html: Open-domain QA. RAG sets a new state of the art on four open-domain QA tasks — Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, and CuratedTREC — beating both extractive models (which can only copy a span from a retrieved passage) and closed-book seq2seq models like T5 (which answer purely from parameters with no retrieval). RAG gets the best of both: it can retrieve and generate free-form, abstractive answers.

Generation and verification. On Jeopardy question generation, RAG produces more specific and factually correct questions than BART alone, because it can ground details in retrieved passages. On FEVER fact verification it lands within a few points of bespoke task-specific architectures, while being a single general model.

The killer practical feature — updating knowledge without retraining. Because the world knowledge lives in the index, not the weights, you can swap the Wikipedia snapshot for a newer one and the model immediately answers differently on facts that changed — no gradient steps, no fine-tuning. The authors demonstrate this by replacing the index and watching answers about (for example) who holds a given office update correctly.

The conceptual payoff: parametric vs non-parametric memory. RAG cleanly separates how to reason and write (parametric, in the generator's weights) from what is true right now (non-parametric, in the swappable index). That split is RAG's lasting contribution: knowledge becomes editable, auditable, and current without touching the model.

pages.title: Why RAG became the dominant LLM application pattern

blocks.html: The default answer. By 2023, 'add RAG' was the standard first response to 'how do we apply an LLM to our private documents?' The original BART + DPR architecture was largely replaced by zero-shot RAG — a frozen, instruction-tuned LLM (GPT-4, Claude) that reads retrieved passages stuffed into its prompt, no joint training required — but the framing came straight from this paper.

The ecosystem it spawned. Modern descendants include hybrid retrieval (combining classic keyword BM25 with dense vectors), rerankers that re-sort candidates, HyDE (generate a hypothetical answer, embed that to retrieve), graph RAG, agentic retrieval (the model decides when and what to search), and the entire vector-database industry — Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma, pgvector — built to be the FAISS index for everyone else.

The enduring lesson. Even as ultra-long-context models reduce the need for retrieval in some cases, the core insight survives: you do not have to cram all knowledge into the weights. Separating a reasoning engine from a searchable, updatable knowledge store is good engineering, and RAG is the paper that made that separation a first-class idea in NLP.
